title: Identifying Logical Operations from Syndrome Histories for qLDPC Codes
authors: Yizhuo Tan, Shifan Xu, Yongshan Ding, Jakub Szefer
abstract: Syndrome histories are normally used to detect and correct errors in fault-tolerant quantum computation, but they can also reveal information about the logical operations executed during computation. We study logical-operation identification using syndrome histories alone or together with other classical measurement outcomes. We develop an exact inference method and a scalable approximation that account for unknown circuit faults and ideal measurement randomness. We evaluate automorphisms, logical Pauli measurements, T injections, and logical circuits combining these instructions on \([[18,4,2]]\) and \([[72,12,6]]\) bivariate bicycle (BB) codes under multiple noise models and error rates. A single logical instruction can be identified with over 94\% accuracy under circuit-level noise with error rates between \(10^ {-5} \) and \(10^{-3}\). We also achieve over 99\% accuracy for automorphism-based logical circuits and 78.32\% for logical circuits combining all three instructions. We further analyze identification ambiguities arising from insufficient or indistinguishable measurement information, fault timing, and approximation inference. Together, these results extend the role of syndromes beyond error decoding to identifying executed logical operations and circuits during fault-tolerant quantum computation. They also suggest that access to syndrome histories and related classical measurement outcomes may unintentionally reveal information about the executed computation.
summary: This paper shows that syndrome histories from quantum error correction codes can be used not just to correct errors, but also to deduce the specific logical operations that were executed. By developing advanced inference methods, the authors achieve high accuracy in identifying complex quantum circuits, suggesting that the measurement record itself is a rich source of information about the computation's history.
main_problem: The paper addresses the problem of identifying which logical operations or circuits were executed during fault-tolerant quantum computation using only syndrome histories or by combining them with classical measurement outcomes.
main_result: The authors achieved high identification accuracies (e.g., >94% for single instructions) by analyzing syndrome histories, demonstrating that syndromes reveal information beyond simple error decoding.
method: They developed an exact inference method and a scalable approximation to calculate candidate likelihoods, accounting for unknown circuit faults and measurement randomness.
model_or_system: The study uses Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes, specifically Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes, to model the physical system undergoing fault-tolerant computation.
key_observables: Syndrome histories (Y), classical measurement outcomes from logical Pauli measurements and T injections, and the identification accuracy (%) of the executed operation.
important_parameters: Error rates between $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-3}$; code sizes like $	ext{[[18,4,2]]}$ and $	ext{[[72,12,6]]]}$
main_assumptions: The methods account for unknown circuit faults and ideal measurement randomness, though ambiguities remain due to insufficient measurement information or approximation limitations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how error transport via automorphisms distinguishes candidate operations (Fig. 1) and compare the results of standard error decoding versus logical-operation identification (Fig. 2).
paper_structure: The work introduces the problem, details the use of syndrome histories and auxiliary measurements, presents the inference methods, evaluates performance on specific codes and operations (automorphisms, Pauli measurements, T injections), and discusses limitations and refinements.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful diagnostic tool for quantum computation, suggesting that the measurement record itself can act as a forensic tool to reconstruct the computational history, which is relevant for understanding decoherence and process verification in quantum hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Error transport can make candidate automorphisms distinguishable. The same detectable Pauli error et is present before either candidate auto- morphism. The two automorphisms transport the error to different data qubits, producing different syndromes at the next SEC.

Fig. 2. Comparison of error decoding and logical-operation identification. (a) Error decoding assumes the executed circuit is known and uses the syndrome history to determine a correction or Pauli-frame update for unknown errors. (b) Logical-operation identification assumes both the executed circuit and errors are unknown, and uses the same syndrome history, optionally supplemented by auxiliary measurement outcomes, to identify the logical operations.

Fig. 3. Coupling across a noisy syndrome history. The circuit interval contains one automorphism operation g followed by syndrome extraction. Interval fault pattern Ft determines new data error ut and measurement error mt. Together with the existing data error et−1 transported by g, these effects determine the current data error et and the measured syndrome yt. Since et becomes input to the next operation-SEC interval, adjacent syndromes are coupled and cannot be scored independently.
